newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Ruling parties claim big win in Yugoslav polls.
newsitem.headline: Ruling parties claim big win in Yugoslav polls.

text.p: A coalition of leftist parties led by Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic was on Wednesday cruising to a parliamentary election victory which officials say will consolidate peace and bring prosperity to the region.

Voters across Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro, went to the polls on Sunday to choose a new federal parliament, a republican assembly for Montenegro and local councils across the federation.
Yugoslavia's ruling coalition claimed a "resounding victory" in the federal elections by winning almost two-thirds of parliamentary seats.
Also good news for Milosevic's camp was the clear majority won by the ruling Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS) of Montenegro in the republican parliament.
The DPS votes together with the allied Serbian left coalition would give Milosevic firm control of the federal parliament.
The leftist coalition comprises Milosevic's Socialist Party (SPS), the Yugoslav United Left (JUL) led by his powerful wife Mirjana, and New Democracy.

The coalition victory would enable Yugoslavia "to take its place among European states, (open) to the world, increase production and improve the standard of living of its people," Yugoaslav deputy prime minister Jovan Zebic said.
"The results are a confirmation of Milosevic's steadfast (peacemaking) policy and of popular endorsement to its continuation," the Yugoslav news agency quoted him as saying.
He categorically denied rumours of post-election devaluation of the national currency dinar and said his government was set on liberalising foreign economic ties.
Yugoslavia is plagued by economic troubles after a four-year war and sanctions but the opposition failed to capitalise on the issue.

"(The coalition) has won a resounding victory. Together with the DPS, it will guarantee another four years of development in peace and a stable functioning of the federal parliament's Chamber of Citizens," ruling coalition spokesman Ivica Dacic said.
Diplomats expect Milosevic, the real power broker in the country, to move next year into the post of federal president vested with sweeping executive powers.

The Montenegrin election commission said the DPS won 45 seats in the (71-seat) Montenegrin assembly, the opposition coalition National Unity 19, the Moslem Party of Democratic Action three and the Democratic Alliance of Montenegro and the Democratic Union of Albanians two seats each.
The count for the 138-seat federal parliament elections where Montenegrins have 30 seats was not complete, but the DPS was also expected to win there.
In Belgrade, Dacic said that, with 80 percent of the vote counted, the left had won at least 64 seats.
The opposition Zajedno (Together) alliance won 22 seats and the ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party 16, he said.
Although the opposition Zajedno coalition fared worse than expected, it claimed a small victory.

"After the disgraceful (state) media blockade, the removal of opponents of the regime from voters' registers and the ejection of our representatives (from polling booths), the result we achieved in these elections is a miracle," Zajedno spokesman Ivan Kovacevic told a news conference.

Opposition officials blamed their poor performance on the tightly-controlled state-run media, a boycott by ethnic Albanians which handed the governing coalition 15 seats, a lack of interest in the West and voter apathy.
